pathophysiology.summary: Toxicity depends on the substance, dose, formulation, time, co-ingestants, and host physiology. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.

Reduced ability to speak or perform usual activity

actions: Escalate treatment and monitoring per local protocol.

prepared.title: Acute Severe Asthma Exacerbation (Adult)
prepared.source_title: Asthma: diagnosis, monitoring and chronic asthma management (BTS, NICE, SIGN)
prepared.scope: Adults who are acutely unwell or highly symptomatic at presentation; limited to immediate treatment, objective testing and post-attack action-plan review.

pathophysiology.summary: An acute exacerbation is a sustained worsening of airflow obstruction caused by bronchial smooth-muscle constriction, airway-wall oedema and mucus plugging on a background of variable airway inflammation. Severe obstruction raises the work of breathing, produces ventilation-perfusion mismatch and may progress from hypocapnia to carbon-dioxide retention as respiratory muscles fatigue.
keyMechanisms: Trigger-driven airway inflammation and bronchial hyper-responsiveness narrow conducting airways.
Mucosal oedema and tenacious secretions amplify expiratory flow limitation and dynamic hyperinflation.
Ventilation-perfusion mismatch causes hypoxaemia; a normalising or rising carbon dioxide level in a distressed patient can indicate fatigue.
Prolonged expiration and air trapping increase intrathoracic pressure and the work of breathing.

symptoms: Rapidly worsening breathlessness
Wheeze or chest tightness
Cough, often after a viral, allergen or irritant exposure
Reduced response to the patient's usual reliever medicine
physicalSigns: Tachypnoea with prolonged expiration
Diffuse expiratory wheeze or, in near-fatal obstruction, a quiet chest
Accessory-muscle use and inability to complete sentences
Tachycardia with reduced peak expiratory flow compared with predicted or personal best
redFlags: Exhaustion, confusion, drowsiness, cyanosis, hypotension or a silent chest
Inability to speak, worsening hypoxaemia or poor respiratory effort despite initial treatment
Normal or rising arterial carbon dioxide in a patient with severe respiratory distress
Previous near-fatal asthma, intensive-care admission or mechanical ventilation

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Abrupt multisystem illness with urticaria, angioedema, hypotension or gastrointestinal symptoms after a likely exposure.
Orthopnoea, inspiratory crackles, raised jugular venous pressure or radiographic congestion rather than predominantly expiratory obstruction.
Pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, venous-thromboembolism risk factors or unexplained hypoxaemia with limited wheeze.
Sudden unilateral pleuritic pain, asymmetric breath sounds and hyper-resonance; tension physiology adds hypotension and tracheal deviation.

ruleIn.testName: Peak expiratory flow
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Peak expiratory flow — Severity of airflow obstruction
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Marked reduction from predicted or documented personal best, with serial improvement after treatment supporting reversible obstruction.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Provides an objective trend when the patient can perform the manoeuvre safely.

ruleIn.testName: Continuous pulse oximetry
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Continuous pulse oximetry — Hypoxaemia
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Reduced oxygen saturation or a need for supplemental oxygen to maintain the locally defined target.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Detects gas-exchange impairment and guides titrated oxygen while avoiding delay to treatment.

ruleIn.testName: Arterial or venous blood gas when severe or deteriorating
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Arterial or venous blood gas when severe or deteriorating — Respiratory failure and metabolic disturbance
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Hypoxaemia; carbon-dioxide retention or acidaemia in life-threatening disease.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: A rising carbon dioxide level can signal fatigue and the need for critical-care escalation.

ruleOut.testName: Chest radiograph when clinically indicated
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Chest radiograph when clinically indicated — Pneumothorax, pneumonia or pulmonary oedema
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No focal alternative pathology in uncomplicated asthma; an abnormality redirects management.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Imaging is selective rather than routine and should not delay immediate bronchodilator treatment.

ruleOut.testName: 12-lead electrocardiogram
ruleOut.modalityTarget: 12-lead electrocardiogram — Acute coronary syndrome or significant arrhythmia
ruleOut.targetCondition: Acute coronary syndrome or significant arrhythmia
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Absence of acute ischaemic change or a clinically important rhythm disturbance.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Useful for older patients, chest pain, marked tachycardia or relevant cardiovascular comorbidity.

clinicalManagement.title: Immediate assessment and stabilisation
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Immediately on arrival
actions: Use an airway-breathing-circulation approach and call senior emergency support for severe or life-threatening features.
Position upright when tolerated, establish monitoring and obtain intravenous access without delaying inhaled therapy.
Give controlled oxygen to the locally approved saturation target and reassess frequently.

clinicalManagement.title: Reverse bronchoconstriction
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Within minutes
actions: Give repeated inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonist using an appropriate delivery system.
Add inhaled ipratropium bromide in severe or life-threatening exacerbation.
Document response using symptoms, respiratory effort, oxygenation and peak flow where feasible.

branches.condition: Poor response or deteriorating physiology
actions: Escalate immediately to a senior emergency/critical-care clinician.
Consider continuous nebulised bronchodilator delivery and intravenous magnesium sulfate under the approved local protocol.

clinicalManagement.title: Treat airway inflammation
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Early in the first hour
actions: Administer systemic corticosteroid promptly unless contraindicated.
Review likely trigger, adherence and recent corticosteroid exposure.
Do not use antibiotics routinely unless bacterial infection is clinically supported.

clinicalManagement.title: Structured reassessment
clinicalManagement.timeframe: After each initial treatment cycle
actions: Repeat respiratory rate, work of breathing, speech, oxygen saturation and peak flow where possible.
Check for complications and alternative diagnoses if the trajectory is not improving.
Escalate for ventilatory support planning before exhaustion or reduced consciousness develops.

clinicalManagement.title: Determine safe disposition
clinicalManagement.timeframe: After sustained clinical response
actions: Admit patients with persistent severe features, oxygen requirement, poor social support or high relapse risk.
Before discharge, verify inhaler technique, provide an individualised written action plan and arrange controller therapy review.
Explain explicit emergency return precautions.

content.title: Adult Essential Hypertension Screening and Confirmation

pathophysiology.summary: Essential hypertension is persistently elevated arterial blood pressure without an identified secondary cause. It is often asymptomatic and increases cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, and kidney risk.
keyMechanisms: Interactions among genetic, renal, vascular, neurohormonal, and environmental factors
Increased systemic vascular resistance and altered sodium-volume regulation
Cumulative pressure-related vascular and target-organ injury

symptoms: Usually asymptomatic
Occasional non-specific headache or dizziness, which cannot establish diagnosis
physicalSigns: Elevated pressure on correctly performed measurement
Possible target-organ disease in established hypertension
Possible clinical clues to a secondary cause
redFlags: Severe elevation with chest pain, dyspnoea, neurological deficit, confusion, visual loss, or acute kidney injury
Pregnancy with elevated pressure or pre-eclampsia symptoms
Abrupt onset, resistant readings, or suspected secondary cause

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Clinic readings elevated but validated out-of-office average not persistently elevated.
Clinic readings may be below threshold while home or ambulatory readings are elevated.
Young onset, abrupt worsening, resistance, relevant medicines, renal or endocrine clues.
Pain, anxiety, acute illness, stimulants, or measurement error; repeat under standardised conditions.

pathophysiology.summary: Periodic health examination is a risk-based preventive-care process rather than a disease episode. It identifies modifiable cardiovascular, metabolic, cancer, infectious, mental-health and functional risks before symptoms or irreversible complications develop, while avoiding screening that has an unfavourable balance of benefit and harm.
keyMechanisms: Age, sex, family history, exposures and comorbidity alter baseline disease probability and screening benefit.
Repeated measurement can detect trajectories in blood pressure, adiposity, glycaemia and lipids before complications emerge.
Evidence-based screening shifts selected cancers and chronic diseases toward earlier diagnosis.
Shared decisions reduce harms from false positives, overdiagnosis and preventive medicines with small net benefit.

symptoms: Often asymptomatic attendance for preventive review
May disclose fatigue, low mood, sleep problems or reduced function during structured history
May report tobacco exposure, inactivity, unhealthy diet or occupational risk
May have overdue vaccination or cancer screening
physicalSigns: Elevated or discrepant blood-pressure readings
Raised body-mass index or waist circumference
Oral-health, vision, hearing or mobility concerns
Abnormal findings requiring conversion from screening to a diagnostic pathway
redFlags: Chest pain, focal neurological deficit, severe breathlessness or syncope discovered during screening
Markedly elevated blood pressure with acute target-organ symptoms
Suicidal ideation or immediate safeguarding concern
Alarm cancer symptoms such as unexplained bleeding, persistent mass or major unintentional weight loss

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Asymptomatic, eligible by age or risk and suitable for a validated screening intervention.
Known diagnosis or repeated abnormal result requiring disease-specific targets rather than screening thresholds.
Symptoms or signs raise pre-test probability and require diagnostic, not screening, tests.
Single clinic value is not confirmed on repeat or out-of-office measurement.
